title: Joule-Thomson Effect
short_intro: The Joule-Thomson effect describes the temperature change of a real gas when it undergoes steady, adiabatic expansion from a high pressure region to a low pressure region through a porous plug or throttling valve. During this process, the total enthalpy of the system remains constant.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of Joule-Thomson effect, inversion temperature, qualitative behavior of real and ideal gases, and applications such as liquefaction of gases.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Mathematical derivation of the Joule-Thomson coefficient using Maxwell's relations, expression for van der Waals gases, inversion temperature derivation, and proof that the coefficient is zero for ideal gases.

prerequisites: First and Second Laws of Thermodynamics
Concept of Enthalpy and Adiabatic Processes
Van der Waals Equation of State for Real Gases

concept_notes.heading: Fundamentals of the Joule-Thomson Effect
bullets: It is a throttling process characterized by constant enthalpy (isenthalpic process), meaning H<sub>1</sub> = H<sub>2</sub>.
When a real gas expands adiabatically from high pressure to low pressure through a porous plug, it may undergo either cooling or heating depending on the initial temperature.
For an ideal gas, the Joule-Thomson coefficient is identically zero because internal energy depends only on temperature and there are no intermolecular forces.

concept_notes.heading: Joule-Thomson Coefficient
bullets: Defined as the rate of change of temperature with respect to pressure at constant enthalpy: μ<sub>JT</sub> = (∂T / ∂P)<sub>H</sub>.
If μ<sub>JT</sub> > 0, the gas cools upon expansion (cooling region).
If μ<sub>JT</sub> < 0, the gas heats up upon expansion (heating region).

concept_notes.heading: Inversion Temperature
bullets: The temperature at which the Joule-Thomson coefficient changes sign is known as the inversion temperature (T<sub>i</sub>).
At the inversion temperature, μ<sub>JT</sub> = 0, and the gas neither cools nor warms upon throttling.
A gas shows cooling only when its temperature is below its inversion temperature for a given pressure.

concept_notes.heading: Behavior of Real Gases (Van der Waals Gases)
bullets: At temperatures below the Boyle temperature, real gases show cooling at low pressures and heating at high pressures.
The maximum inversion temperature for a van der Waals gas is given by T<sub>i,max</sub> = 2a / (bR), where a and b are van der Waals constants and R is the universal gas constant.
Hydrogen and helium have very low inversion temperatures (below room temperature), hence they must be pre-cooled below their inversion temperatures before they can be liquefied by throttling.

derivations.title: Derivation of Joule-Thomson Coefficient using Maxwell Relations
derivations.conditions: Single-component homogeneous system undergoing a constant enthalpy (throttling) process.
steps: Start with the fundamental thermodynamic property relation for enthalpy: dH = TdS + VdP.
Express entropy S as a function of temperature T and pressure P, so that dS = (∂S / ∂T)<sub>P</sub> dT + (∂S / ∂P)<sub>T</sub> dP.
Substitute dS into the enthalpy equation: dH = T [(∂S / ∂T)<sub>P</sub> dT + (∂S / ∂P)<sub>T</sub> dP] + V dP.
Use the Maxwell relation (∂S / ∂P)<sub>T</sub> = -(∂V / ∂T)<sub>P</sub> and the heat capacity at constant pressure C<sub>P</sub> = T(∂S / ∂T)<sub>P</sub>.
Rewrite the enthalpy differential: dH = C<sub>P</sub> dT + [V - T(∂V / ∂T)<sub>P</sub>] dP.
For an isenthalpic process (dH = 0), set the equation to zero and solve for dT / dP at constant H.
derivations.result: \mu_{JT} = \left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial P}\right)_{H} = \frac{1}{C_{P}} \left[ T\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_{P} - V \right]

derivations.title: Joule-Thomson Coefficient for a Van der Waals Gas
derivations.conditions: Low pressures and moderate temperatures where the van der Waals equation applies.
steps: Write the van der Waals equation of state: (P + \frac{a}{V^2})(V - b) = RT.
Expand the equation neglecting higher-order terms in b: PV + \frac{a}{V} - Pb - \frac{ab}{V^2} = RT \implies V \approx \frac{RT}{P} + b - \frac{a}{RT}.
Differentiate volume with respect to temperature at constant pressure: \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_{P} = \frac{R}{P} + \frac{a}{RT^2}.
Substitute this derivative into the general thermodynamic expression for \mu_{JT}: \mu_{JT} = \frac{1}{C_P} \left[ T \left( \frac{R}{P} + \frac{a}{RT^2} \right) - V \right].
Substitute V \approx \frac{RT}{P} + b - \frac{a}{RT} into the expression to simplify terms.
Obtain the final expression for the van der Waals Joule-Thomson coefficient.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Isenthalpic Curves in P-T Plane
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Curves of constant enthalpy plotting Pressure (P) on the y-axis against Temperature (T) on the x-axis, showing a parabola-like envelope enclosing the inversion curve.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The peak of each isenthalpic curve represents the inversion temperature at that pressure. Inside the inversion parabola, μ<sub>JT</sub> > 0 (cooling); outside, μ<sub>JT</sub> < 0 (heating).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in PGT conceptual multiple-choice questions regarding regions of heating and cooling during expansion.

graphs_and_experiments.title: porous plug experiment (Regnault / Joule-Kelvin)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A thermal insulated tube with a porous plug in the middle, fitted with upstream and downstream manometers and thermometers.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Measures the steady-state temperature difference (ΔT) across the plug for a known pressure drop (ΔP) under adiabatic conditions.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct questions on experimental setup, thermal insulation requirements, and verification of isenthalpic nature.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Joule-Thomson Coefficient vs Temperature
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A graph of μ<sub>JT</sub> on the y-axis versus Temperature T on the x-axis, intersecting the zero axis at T<sub>i</sub>.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows positive values at low temperatures (cooling), crosses zero at T = T<sub>i</sub>, and becomes negative at high temperatures (heating).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Testing understanding of inversion temperature and sign conventions of thermal coefficients.

solved_numericals.question: Why does an ideal gas show no temperature change during a Joule-Thomson expansion?
solution_steps: Recall the expression for the Joule-Thomson coefficient: \mu_{JT} = \frac{1}{C_{P}} \left[ T\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_{P} - V \right].
For an ideal gas obeying PV = RT, find \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_{P} = \frac{R}{P} = \frac{V}{T}.
Substitute this into the bracket term: T(V / T) - V = V - V = 0.
solved_numericals.answer: Delta T = 0 because internal energy of an ideal gas depends solely on temperature and there are no intermolecular forces.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the inversion temperature for a gas obeying the van der Waals equation, given that the van der Waals constants are a = 0.364 N m^4 / mol^2 and b = 4.27 \times 10^{-5} m^3 / mol, and R = 8.314 J / mol K.
solution_steps: State the formula for maximum inversion temperature: T_{i} = \frac{2a}{bR}.
Substitute the given values: a = 0.364, b = 4.27 \times 10^{-5}, R = 8.314.

solved_numericals.question: A real gas has a van der Waals constant a = 0.140 N m^4 / mol^2 and b = 3.91 \times 10^{-5} m^3 / mol. Determine whether the gas will cool or heat when throttled from high pressure to low pressure at room temperature (300 K). Assume C_P = 20.8 J / mol K.
solution_steps: Calculate the Joule-Thomson coefficient using the formula: \mu_{JT} = \frac{1}{C_{P}} \left( \frac{2a}{RT} - b \right).
Substitute the values: R = 8.314 J/mol K, T = 300 K, C_P = 20.8 J/mol K.
Compute the first term inside the parenthesis: \frac{2 \times 0.140}{8.314 \times 300} = \frac{0.280}{2494.2} \approx 1.122 \times 10^{-4} m^3/mol.
solved_numericals.answer: mu_{JT} = +3.51 \times 10^{-6} K/Pa (The gas cools upon throttling).

assumptions_and_limitations: The process is strictly adiabatic; no heat enters or leaves the system through the walls or the porous plug.
Steady-state flow conditions are maintained across the throttling device.
Kinetic energy changes of the gas before and after the plug are assumed to be negligible.
Van der Waals approximation fails at very high pressures where higher-order virial coefficients become significant.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Joule-Thomson expansion is an adiabatic free expansion.
common_misconceptions.correct: It is a steady-flow throttling process through a porous plug maintaining constant enthalpy, whereas free expansion is characterized by constant internal energy (U = constant).
common_misconceptions.why: In throttling, external work is done by the upstream fluid and on the downstream fluid, keeping enthalpy constant rather than internal energy.

common_misconceptions.wrong: All gases cool down when expanded through a valve.
common_misconceptions.correct: Gases heat up if their temperature is above their inversion temperature.
common_misconceptions.why: The sign of the Joule-Thomson coefficient depends on temperature relative to T<sub>i</sub>; above T<sub>i</sub>, μ<sub>JT</sub> is negative.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Hydrogen and helium cool at room temperature during throttling.
common_misconceptions.correct: Hydrogen and helium heat up at room temperature.
common_misconceptions.why: Their inversion temperatures are very low (around 204 K for H<sub>2</sub> and 43 K for He), so at 300 K they are well above T<sub>i</sub>.

quick_revision: Joule-Thomson effect is an isenthalpic process (H = constant).
Ideal gases show no Joule-Thomson cooling or heating (μ<sub>JT</sub> = 0).
Inversion temperature is the temperature where μ<sub>JT</sub> changes sign.
Cooling occurs when T < T<sub>i</sub> (μ<sub>JT</sub> > 0); heating occurs when T > T<sub>i</sub> (μ<sub>JT</sub> < 0).
Maximum inversion temperature for van der Waals gas is T<sub>i</sub> = 2a / (bR).
